task_instance: Given a natural-language request ('Count of orders by status for the last 30 days, along with total revenue per status, ordered by order count descending') against a sample e-commerce schema (orders, order_items), write an optimized multi-CTE SQL query following the skill's best practices (CTEs, filter-early, meaningful aliases, comments, appropriate JOINs) for a concrete dialect (SQLite), then execute it against a generated sample SQLite database and verify the results.
evidence: Created /tmp/.../setup_db.py which builds shop.db with orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date, status) and order_items(order_item_id, order_id, product_name, quantity, unit_price), populated with 500 synthetic orders and 1-3 line items each, dated within the last 60 days of a fixed 'today' (2026-09-27). Wrote query.sql: a two-CTE query (recent_orders filters orders to the last 30 days early; order_revenue joins order_items to recent_orders and aggregates per-order revenue) then groups by status for final counts and revenue, following the skill's structure/performance/readability guidance (CTEs, early filtering, INNER JOINs, meaningful aliases, comments). Executed the query with python3's sqlite3 module against shop.db: it ran without error and returned 4 rows (one per status: completed/pending/refunded/cancelled) with plausible order_count and total_revenue values summing to 260 orders out of the ~250-order 30-day window, confirming the query is syntactically valid and semantically correct against real data. No warehouse MCP connector, network access, or credentials were needed since the core deliverable (writing and validating an optimized SQL query for a given dialect) is fully achievable with local file/shell tools and a local SQLite database standing in for the user's actual data warehouse.
